raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a catheter-based strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Its rationale rests on the observation that, in nonrheumatic AF, thrombus formation is disproportionately localized to the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated embryologic remnant with variable contractility, complex lobar anatomy, and flow stasis during AF [1]. Surgical and pathologic data supported the concept that LAA exclusion might reduce embolic events [2,3], while imaging studies later suggested that LAA morphology and appendageal flow may further modify thromboembolic risk beyond clinical scores [4].

Modern percutaneous LAAC began with feasibility experience using endocardial occluders. Early WATCHMAN experience demonstrated transseptal implantation feasibility, followed by the PLAATO program in patients considered suboptimal for warfarin [5,6]. The pivotal PROTECT AF trial randomized patients with nonvalvular AF to WATCHMAN or warfarin and showed noninferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular or unexplained death, but with an early procedural safety signal [7]. Longer follow-up supported durable efficacy and fewer hemorrhagic strokes, while PREVAIL showed improved procedural safety but mixed efficacy results because of low event rates and wide credible intervals [8,9]. Pooled and extended analyses suggested comparable stroke prevention to warfarin, reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, cardiovascular death, and nonprocedural bleeding, balanced against upfront procedural risk [10,11].

Patient selection remains central. LAAC is most often considered in AF patients with elevated CHA₂DS₂-VASc score who have major bleeding, high bleeding risk, intolerance, or a compelling reason to avoid long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC). The ASAP study supported WATCHMAN implantation without a warfarin transition in patients with contraindications to OAC, using dual antiplatelet therapy instead [12]. Real-world registries such as EWOLUTION extended the evidence base to older, higher-risk patients, including many with OAC contraindications, and demonstrated high implant success with acceptable rates of ischemic stroke and bleeding [13]. Experience with non-WATCHMAN devices also expanded: the Amplatzer Cardiac Plug registry and the prospective Amulet observational study showed high procedural success, though device-related thrombus, residual leak, and pericardial complications remained important considerations [14,15].

Device iteration has improved procedural performance. The next-generation WATCHMAN FLX, evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, was designed for full recapture, repositioning, and broader anatomic coverage, with high closure success and low early major adverse events [16]. The Amulet IDE randomized trial compared Amulet with the first-generation WATCHMAN device and demonstrated noninferiority for safety and effectiveness, with superior residual occlusion but more procedure-related complications early in the learning curve [17]. SWISS-APERO, a head-to-head randomized imaging trial, found more frequent residual patency by cardiac computed tomography after WATCHMAN/FLX than Amulet, emphasizing that “complete seal” depends on both device design and imaging modality [18].

The major randomized comparison with contemporary direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) is PRAGUE-17. In high-risk patients, LAAC was noninferior to DOAC therapy for a composite of stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, clinically relevant bleeding, or procedure/device complications [19]. Four-year follow-up preserved noninferiority and suggested less nonprocedural bleeding after LAAC [20]. These data support LAAC as an alternative, not a universal replacement, for anticoagulation; the certainty is strongest in patients with high bleeding risk or prior bleeding rather than in low-risk patients doing well on DOACs.

Complications cluster into procedural and late categories. Periprocedural risks include pericardial effusion or tamponade, vascular complications, device embolization, air or thromboembolism, and procedure-related stroke. Late issues include device-related thrombus (DRT), peridevice leak (PDL), and bleeding from the required postimplant antithrombotic regimen. DRT after WATCHMAN occurred in approximately 3% to 4% of patients in pooled trial datasets and was associated with increased ischemic stroke or systemic embolism [21]. PDL, once considered acceptable if ≤5 mm, is now increasingly recognized as clinically relevant; 5-year analyses associated leaks at 1 year with higher thromboembolic risk [22]. The NCDR LAAO Registry showed that U.S. postapproval practice included older and more comorbid patients than pivotal trials, with high procedural success and lower in-hospital adverse event rates than early trials [23]. One-year NCDR outcomes confirmed that stroke rates were relatively low but mortality and bleeding reflected the frailty and comorbidity burden of treated patients [24].

Postimplant antithrombotic therapy is evolving. Original WATCHMAN protocols used short-term warfarin plus aspirin, then dual antiplatelet therapy, then aspirin alone. Contemporary practice includes DOAC-based, dual antiplatelet, and sometimes single-agent strategies tailored to bleeding risk. NCDR WATCHMAN FLX data suggest dual antiplatelet therapy may be comparable to OAC plus aspirin in selected patients [25]. The ADALA randomized trial suggested low-dose DOAC may reduce thromboembolic and bleeding events compared with dual antiplatelet therapy after LAAC, but sample size was small and larger trials are needed [26]. Procedural success depends on careful transseptal puncture, multimodality sizing, coaxial deployment, leak assessment, and follow-up imaging [27]. Consensus documents emphasize surveillance for DRT/PDL and individualized antithrombotic therapy [28]. Current U.S. and European guidelines endorse percutaneous LAAC primarily for AF patients with stroke risk who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation or high bleeding risk after shared decision-making [29,30].
